title: Pauri 16, sound: panch parvaan
tomorrow: Pauri 16, meaning: the bull is dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday, mukti, and the end of the trusting stanzas. Your line was free, and freeing. Did you help one person across something? Today, a new stretch of Japji begins. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

For eight stanzas, Japji has been a drumbeat of one word: suniai, suniai, suniai, then mannai, mannai, mannai. Short lines, the same opening every time. Now the music changes. Pauri 16 is longer, wider, and it opens with a line you can almost clap to. Say it and it snaps: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan. Two halves, like two footsteps. After this, the stanzas start counting the uncountable: worlds, devotions, fools, names. The stretch ahead is about the countless. But first, today, just the sound of the door into it.
screen: `SUNIAI, MANNAI — A DRUMBEAT.` → `THE MUSIC CHANGES.` → `PANCH PARVAAN, PANCH PARDHAAN.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening line in the original: panch parvaan panch pardhaan. Four words, and two of them the same. Panch, said PUNCH, is the key word. It can mean five, and it also means the chosen ones, the respected ones, the way a village council in Punjab was called a panchayat. Here commentators read it as the chosen ones, though some keep the five: people who have listened and trusted, the ones the last eight stanzas were describing. We'll open that more tomorrow. Parvaan, par-VAAN: accepted, approved, the way a coin is accepted as genuine. Pardhaan, par-DHAAN: foremost, the chief. It's the same word Punjabis still use for the president of a committee. So: the chosen are accepted; the chosen are foremost. Now the next three lines, in paraphrase: the chosen receive honor in the Court of God; the chosen shine even at the doors of kings; the chosen keep their attention on the one Guru. Listen to how the line is built. Panch opens both halves, like a bell struck twice. Parvaan and pardhaan rhyme, both ending on the long aan. That's why it's easy to say and hard to forget. Here the stanza shifts, from the steady beat of the last eight into something that stretches out. Pauri 16 goes on to talk about a bull holding up the earth, and about countless worlds. That's tomorrow. For today, just get the first line into your mouth.
screen: `PANCH — THE CHOSEN ONES.` · `PARVAAN — ACCEPTED.` · `PARDHAAN — FOREMOST.` · `A BELL STRUCK TWICE.` · then, large: `PANCH PARVAAN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan. Slowly the first time, feeling each syllable. Then again, letting the two halves fall like footsteps. Say it three or four times, then let the words go quiet and sit with the rhythm still moving in you. If a thought comes, let panch parvaan bring you back. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 16. It opens with panch parvaan, panch pardhaan: the chosen are accepted, the chosen are foremost.
Your line: panch parvaan. Today, say the line once more while you're walking somewhere, matching the two halves to your steps. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Pauri 16 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning by many Sikhs; its opening line, panch parvaan panch pardhaan, marks the turn from the listening and trusting stanzas to the longer stanzas on creation's countlessness.

fork.setup: you hear panch parvaan, panch pardhaan for the first time. who are the panch, as commentators read it?
options: the chosen ones, who have listened and trusted.
fork.reveal: commentators read panch as the chosen ones, the people the listening and trusting stanzas described; they are accepted and foremost.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 16, line 1: the chosen are accepted, the chosen are foremost.

trapdoor: what you thought: something about the number five.
what it means: the chosen ones, those who listen and trust, are accepted and honored.
what a scholar hears: panch shares the root of panchayat, the council of respected elders; parvaan means accepted as genuine, pardhaan foremost.
